58.t: Buddy Petit's clean round tone and repertoire
58.s: Punch praises Buddy Petit's round tone, soft playing and tunes like Maple Leaf Rag and High Society, with a break for stomach trouble.
58.q: That's right. But he was strong, though. But the fella I only ever liked to play for me was Buddy Petit. I liked his play. I liked the way he played. Round, pretty. He didn't make high notes, but everything he made was clean.

58.t: Did Buddy Petit play that style?
58.s: Miller says Buddy played a nice horn and got more tone, but is unsure about this style.
58.q: No, Buddy played all. He played a nice home. Mm-hmm. I ain't sure like Buddy played this sort of thing. I don't know. Bucket got a hold of him. That's a piece I used to play for him to play. Mm-hmm. He gets more tone out of it, you know. Mm-hmm.

58.s: Miller says Buddy Petit could hold a note long, like F, though not high.
58.q: Oh yeah, this F. She used to be playing.

172.t: Listening to a record for Buddy Petit's style
172.s: While a record plays they debate whether it is Buddy Petit or an imitator; Ridgley says people loved Buddy despite his bad habits.
172.ch: Buddy Petit and brass band reading
172.q: That's funny. It ain't somebody just like you, but that's his style. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. That's just like him. Somebody show him and then imitate him.

172.t: Mutt Carey and Buddy Petit inventing tunes on the bandstand
172.s: Ridgley recalls Mutt Carey thinking up short tunes on the stand and naming them, and says Buddy Petit was good at this too.
172.q: And then, Mutt Carey could sit on the bandstand and the Blackwood playing four hours. He could sit there and think of something, and before we leave there, he would play. You know, just get things together. He'd always come with something and he'd name it, just to give us some more funny name or…

724.t: Playing with Buddy Petit and his style
724.s: Burbank recalls Petit's eight-piece band, out-of-town jobs, low-register melodic style and use of mutes, and how a clarinet fits with it.
724.q: I played with Buddy Petit. At the time I played with Buddy Petit, he had an eight-piece band. And he used to go out of town, all around Muggaloosa. Mm-hmm.

724.t: Buddy Petit's style, band and drummer Sammy Penn
724.s: Buddy played a six-piece band, soft, not a high-note man, and harmonized under Burbank's lead; Penn and George Washington played drums.
724.ch: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
724.q: Yeah. How many trumpet players does Buddy have in his band? Himself. No other? No other. It's a six piece band. Is anybody around that plays anything like Buddy? Sometimes he can count himself. Anybody around that plays anything like Buddy? No.

251.s: Albert remembers Chris Kelly and Buddy Petit, a great trumpeter who lived across the lake, drank, and died young in 1931.
251.ch: Parades, vice and the New Orleans scene
251.q: He was, he was, he was plunging. He was kind of slow. I loved the slowest he called it. Of course, he was there with his high notes. And of course, here's another one. Punching Chris Kelly. You remember when they met? Sure, he used to stop on the corner of my house on the lobby. I used to stop in…

251.t: Visiting Buddy in Covington and trumpet feeling
251.s: Albert visited Buddy in his shack in Covington to talk music; he admires the feeling of players like Punch Miller.
251.ch: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
251.q: To Covington. Right. In Covington. Buddy had an old shack way back in the woods. What would you all talk about? Well, just everything in general. We'd be cooking on his stove and I would share some of his vittles with him, talk about music and at regular procedure, how I'm doing and how you're…

766.t: Buddy Petit playing second under Toca
766.s: Petit could not get jobs, so he accepted second trumpet in Milton's band; Milton also worked with Celestin.
766.q: Yeah. You see, why hire Buddy Petit? Nobody didn't want to hire him no more. I mean, in other words, he couldn't get no job. I heard he wasn't very reliable sometimes. That's when he came to Aquaman during the A-Mone, one day they lined my chance. I told him, I said, I got a first trumpet player. I…

766.t: Buddy Petit's style compared to Armstrong and Kid Rena
766.s: Petit was a soft, sweet-toned trumpeter, better second than first, played no written music, unlike Armstrong or Rena.
766.q: He was a nice trumpet player, Buddy was a nice... In other words he had a different tone I think than any of those trumpet players.

20.t: Buddy Petit, worn down by drink, sits in
20.s: Buddy Petit sits in but plays poorly, and Lee takes the horn back, which upsets them both.
20.q: I mean entertainers, playing this band. And this was, this was band, that time was the talk of New Orleans. We captained everything. Packed and jammed every night. We'd make novels bands in there. Judy's wife's brother, Cornet Creft. Cornet Creft would come and sit in with them. And things was…

175.s: Justin heard Buddy Petit mostly on advertising trucks and in parades, not at his own club.
175.ch: Kid Rena, Kelly and the old trumpeters
175.q: Buddy Petit was very good too. I didn't hear him too very much, not as much as I had listened to Kid Renee or even Chris Kelly because Chris Kelly used to stay out of my neighborhood there. So I used to get a chance to listen to that in practice all the time. But I understand that I think Buddy…

177.s: Giles played a couple of jobs with Petit after he returned from across the lake; he praised Petit's triple-tonguing trumpet.
177.q: I think he went further than Mandeville, but I think he went around Bonk, Louisiana and all different parts. But at the last he stood over there until he come a while and played here until he got sick and he died. Yeah. You know, but he had stood away but he was one of the greatest trumpet players…

999.t: Old man Petit and offers to teach him music
999.s: Old man Petit played with him, and Joe Nichols and a WPA band director each offered him lessons.
999.q: It is a Petit, that's it. Old man Petit. I think it's the old man, it's Buddy's brother or his daddy, one of the two. Now when I tell guys I played with him, they say, man you're older than you are. But the old man was gone during that time, he was just hanging on, you know. Well all the fellas was…

179.t: Peter's soft trumpet lip; second-lining around Algiers
179.s: Peter read anything but lacked the lip to play loud; Dick used to second line near Homer Street, the Masonic and the Elks.
179.ch: Kid Thomas band and dance work
179.q: And then back by the waterworks sometime. Yeah, back there, well that's the Elks. Oh yeah, the Elks. That's the Elks back there. Uh-huh. Yeah, that's where the Elks home is back there. Uh-huh.

253.t: Did bands use the Red Book; Petit's tone and ability
253.s: Hall says Petit read well, was the best trumpeter in his estimation, played mellow within the staff and seemed well schooled.
253.q: No, because practically all these tunes that everybody knew them, you know, so many bands play them, you know. They said we didn't use them. Did Buddy read pretty well? Yeah, Buddy was a musician.

180.t: Buddy Petit's playing and style compared with Bunk, Kid Rainey and Kid Punch
180.s: Buddy Petit's pretty second parts and diminished chords, how his style differed from Bunk's, and other trumpeters' styles.
180.q: Oh yeah, he was a nice, he was a nice drummer. I'll tell you about Buddy Petit, what I love about Buddy Petit. He couldn't make no high notes like Lou Armstrong, but he did make everything that Lou Armstrong made, see. That's one thing about this song, you know. I love that, you know. And he could…

871.t: Buddy Petit's playing, repertoire and Kid Rene
871.s: Petit played cornet by ear, drank hard, played Scott Joplin-type numbers, and rivalled Kid Rene, whose reputation rose above Armstrong's locally.
871.q: Yeah, played cornet. Was he a hard worker or did he? Oh he was a hard worker. He was a hard drinker too. Yeah, he, he, he. Where did he live then, those days when you played? Those days he was living on Durbanie, between St. Anthony and Poggle.

872.t: Request for a portrait of Buddy Petit
872.s: The interviewer asks Gorman about how Buddy Petit played and what he was like personally.

1000.t: Buddy Petit's style and the music that was never written down
1000.s: Petit had his own style and played numbers never written down; Armstrong comparisons come up and he laments no recordings exist.
1000.q: Well, if you'd say some pieces he played, some pieces he played. Some pieces. Yeah, some pieces he played sounds like him, them low down pieces like he used to play. Well at that time the rather music, the jazz, the more jazz you put to it the better you was at that time. Of course the nicer music…

969.t: Buddy Petit's tone, appearance and comparison with Sam Morgan
969.s: Petit was small with a huge tone and played excursion boats; Sam Morgan had a better but rougher band.
969.q: Well, Buddy, as I recall, was on the small side, but had a very, very powerful tone. And Buddy played on the excursion boats running from West End to Mandeville and Lewisburg. I don't know what arrangement he had with the boat people, but I would imagine that they played for practically the cost of…

264.s: Zardis describes Buddy's staff playing, melody, derby mute and quiet band, and compares him with Kid Howard and Bunk.
264.q: Buddy, Buddy's playing was great. Buddy wasn't, what you mean, what I call a high, you know, man that plays high. He doesn't play high at all. But what Buddy plays, he plays in the staff. You know what I mean? And when he play in the staff, I mean, so much melody and harmony through his music, you…

187.t: Playing with Buddy Petit: head arrangements, style, cutting contests
187.s: Petit led a seven-piece head-arranging band, played close to Armstrong, was powerful, and met Rena in wagon contests.
187.q: Yeah Sammy no one better than me. I played just a set in for a couple of nights, a couple of jobs with him, you understand? I wasn't a regular man but Sammy was with him longer than I was. What kind of a band was it to play with, Lewis? What do you mean? Was it an easy band to play with? Who Buddy…

45.t: Working with Buddy Petit in 1921, his band and ragtime
45.s: Williams played about eight months with Buddy Petit after returning from Los Angeles, before joining Sam Morgan; he lists Petit's men and says ragtime became jazz with the same beat.
45.ch: Opening talk: pianists and Buddy Petit
45.q: What kind of tunes did they play? Well, they called it that time Ragtime, you know. Ragtime, then they changed the name to jazz. They brought the same kind of a beat as far as the new bands of present girls. Oh, yeah.

875.t: Buddy Petit's trumpet style and playing
875.s: Howard describes Petit as an open-horn player, sweet but good, with fine fingering and tongue, who played the Red Book numbers at dances and parties.
875.q: Sweet but good. Good. See when I met him, first time I met him it was in Bugalusa. Yeah. Bugalusa. And he was playing a lot of horn then. After that he came back home here and played a trumpet. No way he wasn't too much with that mute. I mean he didn't use that, he played, but he could fingers so…

48.t: Joe Petit, Yank Johnson and loud trombone playing; the Darcys
48.s: Joe Petit's old age recording, loud players like Yank Johnson, and the Darcy brothers in Chicago.
48.q: Joe Petit was a fellow for him. He had a good tone, too, on trombone. And they had another fellow that I played with, Joe Petit, named Yank Johnson. That's Buddy Johnson's brother. That Yank had... They could put some of the powerfulest tones in the trombone. They didn't think about sweetness, you…

287.t: Buddy Petit: great but unrecorded, and sending Morand as substitute
287.s: Buddy Petit was a great trumpeter who never recorded. Always late, he sent Morand to cover jobs across the lake until he arrived on a later train.
287.q: No, he never recorded at all. He used to send me on many jobs, because he'd always be late. So he'd send me to play in his place until he came, like, across the lake, over Mandeville, Bita Springs, different places like that, I'd play until he came over on the later train.

1006.t: Living next to the Marrero family and Buddy Petit's rehearsals
1006.s: Before the war Alexis lived beside the Marreros, where Buddy Petit's band rehearsed, and praises Petit's playing.
1006.q: I lived next door, half a house with Billy Moriah, Simon Moriah, Joe and John Moriah. We were all like a family. Double house. I could hear them over there rehearsing and everything. That's where... Buddy Petit's band was rehearsing in that same house, right next to our house. Simon was playing…

290.t: Buddy Petit and the violinist Joseph Welch
290.s: He knew Buddy Petit and liked his playing, and recalls violinist Joseph Welch.
290.ch: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
290.q: No, that's right. You couldn't... What they did, what they did, they depended on the trumpet and the clarinet to carry this thing along. Yeah. Yeah. Talking about trumpet, do you remember Buddy Petit? Buddy Petit, yeah, I know him good, too.

291.t: Buddy Petit and Kid Rena, and the tune Sand Dunes
291.s: Barnes describes Buddy Petit's playing, compares it with Kid Rena's treatment of Sand Dunes, and likens early Armstrong to Petit.
291.q: Buddy is a wonderful trumpet player. But he played different from Kid Rene, in that he liked to run a lot of different, we used to call that changes, because of his horn. But if you would hear Louis Armstrong's old record, just like listening to Buddy Petit. But I don't mean Louis' late record,…

637.t: Buddy Petit and the borrowed horn
637.s: The interviewer asks about Buddy Petit; Nicholas remembers Buddy and a story about lending him a horn.
637.ch: Brass bands, Buddy Petit and horns
637.q: I said, yeah, I don't know. I'll tell you. And, uh, you might get him regular. But he ain't playing the record now. And there's two same guy brothers crooked. Buddy Petit. Yeah, two same guys.

867.t: Basin Street and the district bands
867.s: Charles remembers Basin Street and the district as before his time, and mentions Buddy Petit among the bands (the transcript degenerates into a repeated-word ASR loop).
867.q: I remember those days. I remember those days. I remember those days. But that was before my time. Yeah, before my time. Yeah, I remember Basin Street. All down in the district. But that was before my time. I had to start playing there. Did they have many bands in the district when you were here?…

801.t: Bunk Johnson and the three trumpeters
801.s: Eddie describes Keppard, Joe Oliver and Bunk as his father's trumpeters, and Bunk's sweet style learned from Buddy Petit.
801.q: He's a third corner player. My daddy's friend. He was the third and the next to the last. The last man was Sam Morgan. Sam Morgan was the last.

832.t: How Buddy Petit played, his California trip and his habits
832.s: Foster describes Buddy Petit's own style, sweet or hot, his trip to California with George Washington where he got sick, and how he lived as a bachelor.
832.q: He was one of the best, or what did you say? He had his own style. He had his own style. He didn't. But he had his own style.

849.t: Buddy Petit and buying his horn from his son
849.s: Joseph recalls Buddy Petit's many bookings and how he bought Petit's first horn from his son, Little Buddy.
849.q: Yeah, I'll tell you. I'll tell you. Yeah, I'll tell you about that. I'll tell you about that. Yeah. I'll tell you about that.

825.s: Ernie praises Buddy Petit as a wonderful trumpeter who played more blues than any other band around and could play almost anything.
825.ch: Early freelance work and New Orleans trumpeters
825.q: do you remember him as yeah playing that way yeah buddy buddy was one he was wonderful uh trumpet player mostly making them diminish cars he was great at that matter of fact most anybody that know him right now and they'll tell you and most of all the musicians at this time they'll tell if he or he…

574.s: Petit stayed in the middle range, no high notes; George Washington on trombone with him.
574.q: Yeah, he'd never catch them fool out with them high notes. Oh, he stayed right in there. Kinda make some hominies, too. I mean, I'm gonna live, him and a little guy by the name of George Washington used to play Trombone with him.
